summary: Background: Patients with infertility often have inadequate reproductive health literacy (RHL), while existing health education materials may be difficult to read, overly complex, and insufficiently tailored to individual needs. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have created new opportunities to improve health education through their ability to generate and interpret medical information. However, their applicability and content quality in infertility education remain insufficiently evaluated. Objective: This study systematically evaluated the readability and content quality of LLM-generated health education materials for patients with infertility, identified model strengths and limitations, and provided evidence to support their standardized use in reproductive health. Methods: This study selected DeepSeek-R1, ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus), Kimi 2.5, Qwen 3, and Gemini 3 as the study subjects. Based on the theoretical framework of RHL, this study developed a standardized question list comprising 6 dimensions and 93 items, and used unified prompts to generate health education texts in both Chinese and English. In this study, the Datayze Readability Analyzer was used to assess readability via the Flesch Reading Ease, Gunning Fog Index, and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Meanwhile, the content quality was evaluated in a double-blinded manner by reproductive medicine experts across 3 dimensions: accuracy, comprehensiveness, and humanistic care. Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to compare performance across the LLMs, and Pearson correlation analysis was conducted to examine the associations between readability and content quality. A radar chart was used to evaluate the overall performance of each model. Results: The 5 LLMs differed significantly in both text readability and content quality. In terms of readability, Gemini 3 and Qwen 3 performed best, with significantly higher FRE scores than the other 3 models. DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi 2.5 performed least favorably, with FKGL scores corresponding to a ninth-grade reading level. ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus) showed intermediate performance. In terms of content quality, Kimi 2.5 performed best across accuracy, comprehensiveness, and humanistic care, followed by DeepSeek-R1. ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus) performed least favorably. Analysis revealed significant negative correlations between readability and content comprehensiveness for texts generated by Kimi 2.5, indicating a trade-off between these 2 attributes. The composite radar chart analysis showed that Kimi 2.5 achieved the highest score (11,594.33), whereas ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Plus) had the lowest score (5555.83). Conclusions: Different LLMs showed significant differences in performance in generating health education texts for patients with infertility. In some models, readability was negatively correlated with content comprehensiveness. Under the conditions of this study, Kimi 2.5 demonstrated strong overall performance. However, no model achieved the best performance across all evaluation dimensions. Future applications of LLMs in reproductive health education will require domain-specific optimization, context-specific adaptation, and systematic quality control to support more accurate, comprehensive, and patient-centered communication.
title: Evaluating the Performance of Five Leading Large Language Models in Generating Health Education Materials for Patients With Infertility: Comparative Analysis

summary: Background: The rapid adoption of generative AI in the community and health care necessitates reliable, human-led evaluation. Objective: This study aimed to develop a standardized rubric to support health care professionals, administrators, and researchers in evaluating generative AI outputs in health contexts. Methods: A rubric was developed through a 4-stage mixed methods study: literature synthesis, expert refinement, pilot application, and post-pilot feedback. The rubric was informed by 69 publications and refined through iterative feedback from a multidisciplinary expert panel (n=23). The pilot rubric was applied to 4 health care scenarios: responses to health-related Reddit questions, generation of health-related images and videos, responses to health professional continuing education questions, and automated physician-to-physician clinical documentation generation. Via these scenarios, 15 clinicians (medical practitioners, pharmacists, and medical oncologists) evaluated 250 input-output pairs using domain-level ratings and qualitative comments. The evaluated outputs included 200 AI-generated responses across the 4 health care scenarios and 50 physician-tagged replies in the health-related Reddit questions scenario. Results: The final rubric, OMNI, comprised 10 evaluation domains (Accuracy, Safety, Recognizes Uncertainty, Completeness, Communicates Clearly, Empathetic, Context Aware, Referencing, Follows Instructions, and Avoids Coerciveness) assessed on 4-point Likert scales, supported by detailed instructional and example materials. Via the 4 pilot scenarios, assessors generated 9600 domain-level ratings and 4010 qualitative comments. The mean pairwise agreement for the 4-point Likert groups ranged from 30.8% to 53.4%, increasing to 59.3% to 79.6% when collapsed into broad agreement categories; Gwet’s AC2 ranged from 0.49 to 0.80. OMNI differentiated strengths and weaknesses between models within scenarios, while recurrent limitations in Referencing, Recognizes Uncertainty, Completeness, Empathetic, and Accuracy were identified across scenarios. Multimodal image and video outputs had the highest occurrence of negative rating domains. Assessors reported OMNI was usable and indicated they would reuse it. Conclusions: OMNI is a standardized, accessible rubric for expert-led evaluation of generative AI outputs in health contexts. Pilot application demonstrated that OMNI could differentiate AI performance across models and domains while generating structured feedback. Further work is needed to assess its applicability to purpose-built health AI tools, agentic systems, and organizational evaluation settings.
title: Development and Pilot Evaluation of a Standardized and Accessible Rubric (OMNI) for Assessing Generative AI in Health Care Contexts: Four-Stage Mixed Methods Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Health care systems increasingly promote patient engagement and self-management through digital health services. Digital care pathways, which support coordinated care delivery across the patient journey, have emerged as a promising approach, although evidence regarding their impact on resource use and costs remains limited. <strong>Objective:</strong> The aim of this study was to examine the implementation and impact of digital care pathways specifically designed to reduce or replace physical contacts or phone consultations in specialized health care. <strong>Methods:</strong> We analyzed the 10 most widely used digital care pathways by user volume. The selection criteria were (1) more than 1500 users per digital care pathway and (2) the aim of replacing or reducing in-person contacts. Descriptive analyses quantified digital contact volumes, average contacts and costs per patient, and inflation-adjusted expenditures using the consumer price index, both overall and by patient group. Ecologic group-level correlations were examined to assess whether the 2024 proportion of digital contacts was associated with changes in physical contacts and total costs from 2018 to 2024. <strong>Results:</strong> Digital care pathways were progressively adopted between 2018 and 2024, increasing from no use to accounting for 19.1% (34,837/182,188) of all outpatient contacts among the studied patient groups. Physical visits declined from 74.8% (99,201/132,622) to 54.1% (98,642/182,188), while contacts per patient rose by 7.6% on average. Conditions with the highest uptake of digital pathways showed the strongest reductions in the share of physical visits per patient, with declines of up to 39.7% (0.73/0.44). Average outpatient costs per patient decreased by 18.2% (€421/€515; €1=US $1.12 as of Oct 16, 2026) in real terms, with a 39.3% (€233/€384) reduction in the costs of physical contacts and a 15.4% (€135/€117) increase in the costs of phone visits. Digital pathway contacts accounted for 12.6% (€53/€421 per patient) of total outpatient costs in 2024; however, only 8.8% of the variance in total cost levels was explained by digital pathway adoption, suggesting that the shift toward digital care pathways did not substantially drive overall cost changes. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Digital care pathways expanded rapidly, reaching nearly one-fifth of all outpatient contacts by 2024 in the included patient groups and contributing to a notable reduction in physical visits. However, their overall cost impact remains uncertain, as there have also been other factors impacting the development of outpatient costs. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong>
title: Implementing Digital Care Pathways and Changes in Contact Volume, Contact Distribution, and Outpatient Costs in Specialized Health Care: Retrospective Longitudinal Observational Study
At Your Fingertips and on Your Mind? Digital Health Engagement and Psychological Distress

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to causal explanation in public health and epidemiology. However, recent studies suggest that LLMs exhibit instability in processing temporal information, which raises concerns about their suitability for generating coherent causal explanations. Despite this, little is known about how distinct components of temporal information influence LLM-generated causal explanations in epidemiological contexts. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to examine how event ordering and the validity and presence of explicit temporal information affect LLM-generated causal explanations of long-term lung cancer incidence trends. Specifically, we evaluated their effects on evidence grounding, causal alignment, and disease specificity. <strong>Methods:</strong> We used a 2×3 factorial design manipulating event ordering (chronological vs randomized) and explicit temporal information (accurate, inaccurate, or absent). Five LLMs (GPT-5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8, Qwen3-32B, and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct) generated 600 causal explanations of long-term lung cancer incidence trends using Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) data and PubMed-derived event statements. The effects of ordering and information were assessed using regression and factorial ANOVA. <strong>Results:</strong> Randomized ordering showed higher evidence grounding than chronological ordering (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.53, 95% CI 1.89-3.37; <i>P</i><.001). Causal alignment was higher under chronological than randomized ordering across all 3 information conditions, with larger differences in the decreasing phase. Disease specificity was higher under randomized ordering only under accurate information. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> More accurate or structured temporal information did not necessarily improve LLM-generated causal explanations. Randomized ordering was associated with greater evidence utilization, whereas chronological ordering supported causal alignment across all information conditions, particularly for decreasing trajectories. These findings suggest that temporal context should be structured not only to provide temporal information but also to support the intended characteristics of the resulting explanation.
title: Effects of Temporal Information Structure on Causal Explanations Generated by Large Language Models: Experimental Study Using Lung Cancer Incidence Data

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> The accurate detection of clinical symptoms in electronic health records (EHRs) is pivotal for advancing large-scale genetic and longitudinal studies in psychiatry. Free-text clinical notes are an essential source of symptom-level information, particularly in psychiatry; however, the automated extraction of symptoms from clinical text remains challenging. <strong>Objective:</strong> We aimed to evaluate the ability of open-source generative large language models (LLMs) to detect psychiatric symptom-level concepts from clinical text in Spanish and to develop a new fine-tuned, open-source LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information. <strong>Methods:</strong> We tested 11 open-source generative LLMs for their ability to detect 109 psychiatric concepts from clinical text, using annotated EHR notes from a psychiatric hospital in Colombia. The LLMs were evaluated both “out-of-the-box” and after fine-tuning and compared against a traditional natural language processing (tNLP) method developed from the same data. To develop a fine-tuned LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information, we created a novel synthetic dataset, leveraging real concept annotations while generating fully synthetic clinical text, and fine-tuned a top-performing LLM on these data. Fine-tuned model generalizability was assessed through cross-site evaluation using data from a second independent hospital in Colombia. <strong>Results:</strong> We show that while base LLM performance was poor to moderate (zero-shot: 0.2-0.6 macro-<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>; few-shot: 0.2-0.74 macro-<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>), it improved significantly after fine-tuning (0.75-0.86 macro-<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>), with several fine-tuned LLMs outperforming the tNLP method. In total, 100 psychiatric concepts could be reliably detected (<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>>0.8) using either a fine-tuned LLM or tNLP. Using the synthetic dataset, we developed Mistral-small-psych, a new LLM capable of detecting psychiatric concepts from Spanish clinical text with performance comparable to models trained on real EHR data (macro-<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>=0.79) while remaining fully distributable. In cross-site evaluations, most LLMs generalized well, with small out-of-domain performance losses (macro-<i>F</i><sub>1</sub> decrease of 0.02-0.16). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This work provides the first large-scale, cross-institutional evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs for psychiatric concept detection in Spanish EHRs, introduces a privacy-preserving pathway for building shareable clinical natural language processing models, and presents a new open model for extracting symptom-level psychiatric information from Spanish clinical text.
title: Generative Large Language Models for Psychiatric Concept Detection in Spanish-Language Electronic Health Records: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Screen use is almost universal, and numerous studies have highlighted both the benefits and the risks of this digital integration. However, evidence on the association between screen time and health outcomes among university students remains inconsistent. Substantial methodological variation has limited the synthesis and interpretation of existing findings. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to (1) quantify the associations between screen time and health outcomes as primary analysis; (2) quantify the association between screen time and physical (sleep quality, eye health, weight-related) and mental health outcomes (depression, psychological distress/stress, combined mental health, and well-being); and (3) identify study-level characteristics that explain between-study heterogeneity by using subgroup and meta-regression analyses. <strong>Methods:</strong> PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched, with final searches conducted on July 11, 2026, and reference lists were additionally screened. Eligible studies included university students aged 17 years or older, assessed screen time as duration, and reported physical or mental health outcomes with sufficient statistical data for effect-size calculation. We followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) checklist. Data were synthesized in RStudio using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustments. Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions was examined. Small-study effects, leave-one-out, and influence diagnostics were also conducted. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 82 studies (83 independent samples; 161,340 participants) were included. Longer screen time duration was significantly associated with poorer health outcomes overall (k=83; <i>r</i>=0.175, 95% CI 0.133-0.217; <i>P</i><.001; 95% prediction interval –0.184 to 0.493), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (<i>I</i><sup>2</sup>=98.35%; Q<sub>82</sub>=4744.45; <i>P</i><.001). Pooled associations were similar for mental health (k=38; <i>r</i>=0.176, 95% CI 0.124-0.227) and physical health outcomes (k=45; <i>r</i>=0.177, 95% CI 0.108-0.243) and broad health domain did not significantly moderate the association (<i>P</i>=.96). Within mental health, outcome type significantly moderated the association (<i>P</i>=.03). The association was the strongest for depression (k=21; <i>r</i>=0.230, 95% CI 0.167-0.291) and was weaker for well-being (k=7; <i>r</i>=0.040, 95% CI –0.146 to 0.223). Combined mental health outcomes were also significant (k=8; <i>r</i>=0.170, 95% CI 0.076-0.261), whereas stress was not (k=2; <i>r</i>=0.103, 95% CI –0.222 to 0.407). Within physical health, screen time was significantly associated with poorer sleep quality (k=26; <i>r</i>=0.120, 95% CI 0.083-0.158) and eye health outcomes (k=16; <i>r</i>=0.277, 95% CI 0.089-0.446), but not weight-related outcomes (k=3; <i>r</i>=0.071, 95% CI –0.222 to 0.351); differences across physical outcome types were not significant. Study-level moderators did not meaningfully explain the remaining heterogeneity. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Greater screen time was associated with poorer health outcomes among university students, but the magnitude of association varied across specific outcomes and substantial unexplained heterogeneity remained. The predominance of cross-sectional designs, self-reported screen time, and sparse evidence for some outcomes limits causal inference and precision. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs and standardized measurement approaches. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> PROSPERO CRD42024539034; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024539034
title: Association of Screen Time With Physical and Mental Health in University Students: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
From Robots to Organizations: The Role of the AI Scientist

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Dementia is a growing health burden worldwide; however, scalable, low-cost strategies for early risk identification are lacking. Because cardiac and cognitive aging are closely associated, a routinely collected 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), interpreted using foundation model embeddings, is a promising and accessible candidate marker. However, it is unclear whether such embeddings carry predictive information independent of chronological age—the dominant risk factor for dementia—and whether the underlying changes follow a detectable prediagnostic trajectory. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to investigate whether foundation model embeddings of routine ECGs carry information that distinguishes patients later diagnosed with cognitive impairment or dementia from matched controls, beyond chronological age, and, if so, whether the underlying ECG changes intensify as diagnosis approaches. <strong>Methods:</strong> In a retrospective two-site Korean cohort (Severance Hospital, development n=52,355; Yongin Severance Hospital, external n=6500), embeddings from the knowledge-enhanced diagnosis foundation model supported an ECG-only classifier that discriminated patients diagnosed with cognitive impairment or dementia within the following 10 years from matched controls, using only ECGs interpreted as normal sinus rhythm. We compared an age-only model with a late fusion of age and ECG-derived probability and tested whether age-residualized embedding is predictive as direct evidence of age-independent information. Discrimination was summarized by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) with 95% bootstrap CIs, and DeLong tests and net reclassification improvement (NRI) were used for between-model comparisons. To trace the prediagnostic time course, we analyzed ECG phenotype labels across four windows before diagnosis in an exact-age-matched case-control set. <strong>Results:</strong> Chronological age strongly discriminated cases from controls in both cohorts (external AUROC 0.809, 95% CI 0.799-0.819). Adding ECG-derived probability improved discrimination, calibration, and net benefit over age alone (external AUROC 0.825, 95% CI 0.816-0.834; DeLong <i>P</i><.001; positive NRI). Critically, even after removing the age-predictable component, age-residualized embedding retained modest but reproducible discrimination in both internal (AUROC 0.590, 95% CI 0.581-0.599) and external (AUROC 0.579, 95% CI 0.567-0.592) validation (both <i>P</i><.001), indicating dementia-relevant information that was not explained by chronological age. Of the 105 ECG labels, 19 (18.1%) showed a case-control difference that widened significantly toward diagnosis, dominated by nonspecific ST segment and T wave changes, acute ischemic patterns (acute myocardial infarction), and atrial and junctional arrhythmias (atrial flutter, ectopic atrial, and accelerated junctional rhythms), with divergence emerging mainly in the proximal (1-3-year) and imminent (0-1-year) windows. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Routine ECG foundation model embeddings encode aging-related electrophysiological information that is complementary to and not fully explained by chronological age and intensifies as diagnosis approaches, with concurrent shifts toward ischemic and arrhythmic ECG patterns whose mechanism cannot be determined from these data. These findings suggest that routine ECG is a low-cost, age-complementary triage signal for cognitive impairment and dementia screening, rather than a stand-alone diagnostic test.
title: Electrocardiogram Embeddings Beyond Chronological Age for Prediagnostic Cognitive Impairment and Dementia: Development and External Validation Study

summary: The ethics of autonomous clinical AI are controversial. Traditional ethics assessments have focused on AI model performance rather than health system outcomes. Nichol and colleagues translate established research ethics principles into 9 practical recommendations for trials of autonomous clinical AI. Their findings support an evolution in clinical trial design. The accuracy and performance of the model is important, but the ethical unit of evaluation should be the complete care pathway, with prespecified obligations for subgroup performance, follow-up care, system failures, and model change.
title: The Ethics of Autonomous Clinical AI: Shifting From Model Accuracy to Model Impact
